A LITTLE GUIDANCE GOES A LONG WAY

Make yourself
at home.

Your template is a starting point. Here’s how to turn it into a website that feels like you.

01. Open your template.

Download an individual template or unzip the whole collection. Each design is a single HTML file with its CSS, original SVG artwork, and any JavaScript included. Double-click the file to open it in your browser. There is nothing to install.

02. Find your words.

Open the file in a plain text or code editor. Look for the page’s headings, paragraphs, and navigation links inside the <body>. Replace the demo copy with your own. Update the <title> and the description in the <head>, too.

<title>Your business — Your short tagline</title>
<h1>Your next big idea.</h1>
<p>Tell visitors what makes it matter.</p>

03. Add your own style.

Colors, spacing, and typography are defined in the embedded <style> block. Most templates use CSS variables near the beginning of this block. Edit those values first for a quick visual change. The illustrations are inline SVG, so they don’t depend on a separate image host.

To replace an illustration with your own image, put the image beside your HTML file and use an image element such as <img src="your-image.jpg" alt="A clear description">. If you use images or fonts from other sources, check their licenses before publishing.

04. Connect the real things.

The templates include illustrative business content and local demonstrations. Replace example email addresses, dates, speakers, product names, and prices with your real details. Connect a payment service, mailing list provider, or backend if your site needs one.

Sunday’s bag, Chapter’s signup, Gather’s attendance inquiry, and Signal’s plan selector are front-end demonstrations. They do not process payments, send messages, create accounts, or register attendees.

05. Check, then publish.

  1. Save your changes and refresh the browser.
  2. Resize the window and test on a phone. Check every link, navigation item, and interaction.
  3. Rename your finished template to index.html.
  4. Upload the file and any added assets to a static hosting service of your choice.

Your finished website does not require a build step or a JavaScript framework.

Yours to build on.

The templates and original SVG artwork are available under the MIT license. You can use them for personal projects, client work, and commercial websites. Keep the copyright and license notice in your source files.
